seo_title: Mono Grande explained: the de Loys ape photo and the legend
seo_desc: Mono Grande means big monkey. The South American ape story from Venezuela and Colombia, the 1920 de Loys photo, and why experts say it shows a spider monkey.
summary: A big, tailless ape said to live in the forests of Venezuela and Colombia, best known from one 1920s photo that experts say shows a spider monkey.
body: Mono Grande just means 'big monkey' in Spanish, and that's pretty much the whole claim. People in the forests of northern South America (Venezuela, Colombia and the Guianas) have told stories about a large, tailless ape where no apes are known to live. Alexander von Humboldt heard about hairy wild people called salvajes on the Orinoco around 1800 and he didn't believe a word of it.

The most famous piece of evidence is a photograph taken by Swiss geologist François de Loys during an expedition near the Colombia-Venezuela border around 1920. It shows a dead, upright-propped animal his party had shot. Anthropologist George Montandon published it in 1929 and named it a new species.
Experts quickly identified the animal as a spider monkey with its tail hidden or removed, and the photo is now widely considered a hoax. Similar photos appeared in the 1950s.
